source.title: Interpolating Predictors in High-Dimensional Factor Regression
source.authors: F. Bunea; Seth Strimas-Mackey; M. Wegkamp

record.tranche_reason: The study tests post-interpolation risk behavior with minimum-norm regression predictors in factor-regression settings, rather than with deep networks or the original study's full set of sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper gives theoretical risk bounds, but those bounds are not themselves sweeps across model size, epochs, or sample size. The simulation figures sweep p/n and report excess risk; their plotted values are not stated numerically. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyses minimum-norm interpolating least squares under a latent factor regression model, a setting the originals did not use. Its simulations sweep γ = p/n and show excess risk peaking at γ = 1 and then descending, which bears on V4. Theorem 1 and the regularized comparators in Figure 2 also bear on V4's scope and on V6's regularization clause.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the minimum-norm interpolator is not useful when the effective rank of Σ_X far exceeds n, since its risk approaches the null risk. Under a factor regression model with effective rank below n, its excess risk can vanish despite interpolation, and it is competitive with PCR and CV-tuned ridge for large p/n. In simulations its risk peaks at γ = 1, where regularized methods show no peak.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes minimum-norm least-squares prediction in latent factor regression and shows p/n simulations; it does not reproduce deep-network size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The simulated risk curve differs across the reported factor-loading settings: a randomly generated loading matrix in Figures 1–2 versus a sparse canonical-basis loading matrix in Figure 4. Figure 2 also compares against regularized predictors, whose curves are reported not to have the GLS peak.
record.problems: The curve values in the figures are not stated numerically, and the simulations vary K and n along with p. The reported sweep evidence is specific to the paper's factor-regression simulation settings.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported comparator rows were included: PCR, LASSO, ridge, and the null predictor are comparisons, and the paper says the regularized methods do not interpolate at the peak. The comparison does not test the claimed curve for the interpolating predictor under regularization.

untested.parts: Deep networks; model-size sweeps at fixed n.
Sample-size sweeps near the interpolation threshold.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise or variance dependence of the peak; multiple peaks.
No recounting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Theorem 1: when r_e(Σ_X) > C·n, the min-norm interpolator's risk ratio to the null risk approaches 1 (bounded by sqrt(n/r_e)). Post-interpolation risk is then no better than predicting 0.

Excess-risk curves of ridge (CV-tuned), LASSO (CV-tuned) and PCR across γ, which show no peak at γ = 1 while GLS peaks. Ridge approaches GLS risk for large γ, suggesting the optimal ridge penalty tends to 0. These should be rows for the regularization clause of V6, not left out as comparators.

record.verdict_notes: Changed tranche from T2 to T3: min-norm linear regression under a factor model is a new setting rather than a different method for the originals' question. All simulation sweeps vary K, n and p jointly (n = floor(K^1.5)), so γ is not a pure capacity axis at fixed n. Curve values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Changing training sample size near interpolation.
The study tests p/n sweeps for minimum-norm regression in factor-regression simulations, not the generality of the curve across all model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across axes.
The study does not sweep label noise, test for multiple peaks, or tune regularization on the same interpolating predictor to test peak disappearance.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number is tested.

relationships.condition: Minimum-norm least squares under factor regression, simulations sweeping γ = p/n (dense random, orthogonal and sparse canonical loadings)
relationships.reason: Excess risk falls again past γ = 1 toward zero: a stated peak at γ = 1 in Figure 2 (r2), and descent in Figures 1 and 4 (r1, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Excess risk peaked at γ=p/n=1 and declined toward zero as capacity increased beyond it.

relationships.condition: Min-norm interpolation when the effective rank of Σ_X is much larger than n (e.g. well-conditioned Σ_X, p >> n)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, as no row records it: Theorem 1 shows R(α̂)/R(0) → 1, so post-interpolation risk only approaches the trivial null risk. A good second descent needs joint low-dimensional structure.
relationships.display_finding: R(α̂)/R(0) approached 1, so risk approached the null baseline; better performance required joint low-dimensional structure.

relationships.condition: Ridge and LASSO tuned by cross-validation, and PCR, in the Figure 2 factor-regression simulation
relationships.reason: Based on the text, as no row records it: the peak at γ = 1 is 'not present in the PCR, LASSO and Ridge risks'. The authors attribute this to regularization.
relationships.display_finding: PCR, LASSO, and ridge lacked the peak at γ=1, which the authors attributed to regularization.
